bull_thesis:
The bull case is that Figma's shares were broken by plumbing rather than by business decay, and that the plumbing has a contractual end date four trading days away.

Start with the business, because the whole case rests on it being healthy. Revenue in the quarter ended 31 March 2026 was $333.4 million, up 46% from a year earlier -- and that growth rate went 38%, then 40%, then 46% across the last three reported quarters. It accelerated during exactly the months the market was pricing the company as roadkill. Net dollar retention, which measures how much existing customers spend now versus a year ago, reached 139%, the highest in more than two years. Management raised full-year 2026 guidance to $1.422-1.428 billion, about 35% growth, and lifted adjusted operating income guidance to $125-135 million. Free cash flow over the last four reported quarters totals about $237 million. Cash and short-term investments stood at $1.638 billion against $56.2 million of debt, so roughly $3.00 a share of net cash and no solvency question of any kind.

Now the plumbing. Figma came public on 31 July 2025 with a very small tradable float and an unusually elaborate lock-up -- the window during which insiders and pre-listing investors are barred from selling. The original 180-day lock-up ran out on 27 January 2026. A second agreement signed on 30 August 2025 covering about 54.1% of the Class A shares set up four further releases tied to earnings dates: about 38.9 million shares in November 2025, 44.4 million in February 2026, 61.1 million in May 2026, and the final and largest tranche of about 77.7 million shares at the open on the second trading day after the June-quarter report. The company confirmed on 15 July 2026 that it reports after the close on Wednesday 5 August 2026, which fixes that final release at Friday 7 August 2026.

The bull sequence is therefore simple and dated. Ten months of near-continuous, price-insensitive supply from venture funds distributing stock to their limited partners ends permanently on 7 August. What is left is a business growing in the high-30s with 139% retention, a $1.6 billion cash pile, an engaged activist (Findell Capital, whose June 2026 letter demands the product line be cut from eight offerings to four and carries a $40 target), and a share register finally free to be set by fundamental buyers rather than by mechanical sellers. The stock closed 31 July 2026 at $24.32, about 83% below its first-month peak of $142.92 and 26% below its $33 offering price, valuing the operating business at roughly 7.9 times this year's guided revenue. Sentiment does not need to improve for that to re-rate toward $29-30; the selling merely has to stop.

The conditions this case requires: the 5 August print must confirm the guided $348-350 million and roughly 40% growth; the 7 August release must be absorbed in days rather than months; and the market's fear that generative artificial intelligence makes design software unnecessary must stay a narrative rather than showing up in the retention numbers.
bear_thesis:
The bear case is that the event points the wrong way, the entry price has already moved against us, and the floor underneath the position is demonstrated rather than defined.

Direction first. A forced-seller trade pays when a known seller is exhausted and the price is then free to rise. What is contractually certain on 7 August 2026 is not exhaustion -- it is the arrival of permission to sell for about 77.7 million shares, roughly 15% of the ~528 million shares outstanding and a far larger share of what actually trades daily. These holders are pre-listing venture funds, which typically distribute stock in kind to their limited partners, who then liquidate on their own schedule with no reference to price. That is why each of the three earlier tranches produced weeks of drift rather than a single clean flush. Buying on 3 August is buying four days ahead of the largest wave of supply in the company's public life, not after it.

Price second, and this is decisive. The board file underwrites a $29.00 target, a $17.50 floor and a reward-to-risk multiple of 2.85. Those three numbers are only mutually consistent at a share price near $20.49 -- roughly where the stock sat when the file was struck. Since then it has rallied about 46% off its $16.60 record low to $24.32. Against the verified $16.60 low the same target now gives about 19% of upside versus about 32% of downside, a ratio of roughly 0.6 to 1 pointing the wrong way. The rally did not confirm the thesis; it consumed it.

Third, there is no real floor. This is not a signed merger, not a company trading below net cash, not a liquidation. Net cash of about $3.00 a share is 12% of the price and backstops nothing. The only thing under the stock is the $16.60 printed in early July 2026 and re-tested to form a double bottom -- a level the market recently paid, not a level anything prevents it going through. At $16.60 the operating business would be valued at about 5.0 times this year's guided revenue and 4.1 times the roughly $1.76 billion the street models for 2027, which is a perfectly reachable price if the terminal-value argument gains any further ground.

Fourth, the economics behind the growth are deteriorating. Reported gross margin has fallen from about 92% in late 2024 to 79.4% in the March 2026 quarter; some of that is post-listing stock compensation in cost of revenue, but part is the cost of serving artificial-intelligence features and does not reverse. Stock-based compensation was $169.0 million in that single quarter, about 51% of revenue; the activist's own full-year estimate is 27% of revenue against 8% at Adobe. The share count went from 474.8 million to 523.5 million in a year, about 10%. So the claim that the overhang clears for good on 7 August is wrong in a specific way: the contractual overhang clears, the structural issuance of roughly a tenth of the company a year does not.

Finally, the secular fear is live and the market acts on it without warning. Shares fell about 16.5% in the week to 24 July 2026 on generative-artificial-intelligence displacement worry with no company news at all, after a competing design tool launched in April 2026. The sell side has been walking its target down, from about $40 in March 2026 to roughly $30.40 in late July, on a book of four Buys, one Outperform and eight Holds. What confirms this case: any deceleration below the guided 40% on 5 August, retention slipping from 139%, or the 7 August tape showing heavy volume with the price giving back the July rally.
sop_bull:
Event-win value of about $30 a share.

Figma reports as a single operating segment, so the parts here are the operating franchise plus the balance sheet rather than separable divisions.

Operating franchise: if the 7 August release is absorbed quickly, growth holds in the mid-30s and the displacement fear fades from the multiple, the business supports about 8.5 times the roughly $1.76 billion of revenue the street models for 2027. That is $14.96 billion, or about $28.30 a share on ~528 million shares. Eight to nine times forward revenue is where high-30s-growth software with 139% net dollar retention and positive adjusted operating income has historically cleared, and it is still well below the 12-plus times the stock carried at listing.

Balance sheet: $1.638 billion of cash and short-term investments less $56.2 million of debt is about $1.58 billion of net cash, or $2.99 a share. Add it at face value; it is real, liquid and unencumbered.

Total: roughly $31 a share, which I round down to $30 to allow for the ~10% annual share issuance that continues regardless of the lock-up. The street's mean target of $30.40 and the board file's $29.00 sit inside this range; the activist's $40 assumes the cost programme is adopted, which is not in this number.
sop_bear:
Verified downside floor of about $16.60 a share -- and it is a soft one.

Operating franchise: on a decelerating growth rate and a permanently lower gross margin, the business is worth about 4 times the roughly $1.76 billion of 2027 street revenue, which is where unprofitable software with a contested end-market has been trading in this de-rating. That is $7.04 billion, or about $13.30 a share.

Balance sheet: the same $2.99 a share of net cash.

Total: about $16.30, which reconciles almost exactly with the $16.60 record low actually printed in early July 2026 and re-tested weeks later. That coincidence is the strongest evidence available that this level is where the market clears the bear case, and it is why I use $16.60 rather than the $17.50 carried in the board file.

The critical caveat: nothing contractual defends this level. There is no merger consideration, no cash-per-share close to the price, no recovery value. Net cash is only 12% of the current price. This is a demonstrated floor, not a defined one, and a genuine break in the retention numbers on 5 August would take it out.
sop_breakdown:
Probability-weighted between the two outcomes, because no contractual payout exists to anchor to.

Win case $30 (45% odds): the operating franchise at about 8.5 times the roughly $1.76 billion of 2027 street revenue, about $28.30 a share, plus $2.99 a share of net cash. Requires the 5 August print to hold the guided $348-350 million and roughly 40% growth, and the 7 August supply to be absorbed inside a few weeks.

Loss case $16.60 (55% odds): the same franchise at about 4 times 2027 revenue, about $13.30 a share, plus the same $2.99 of net cash -- reconciling to the low the market actually printed in July 2026.

Weighted: 0.45 x $30 + 0.55 x $18 (the loss path realistically stalls between the floor and the current price rather than pinning the low) gives about $23.40. I carry $23, with a range of $21-25.

The uncomfortable conclusion of that arithmetic is that the 31 July close of $24.32 is already slightly above the probability-weighted value. The odds are tilted to the loss case not because the business is weak but because the largest supply event is still ahead and the price has already run 46% off the low into it.
risk_reward: About 0.6 to 1, against us. From the 31 July 2026 close of $24.32, upside to the $29.00 event-win target is about +19% (+25% to the $30.40 street mean); downside to the verified $16.60 floor is about -32%, and that floor is sentiment and valuation rather than contract. The board file underwrote 2.85 to 1, which is only arithmetically consistent at a share price near $20.49 -- the level the stock traded at before the July rally. The asymmetry has been spent, not earned. Reward-to-risk returns to roughly 2.5 to 1 below about $20.10, which is the level to work with.
catalyst_summary: The final contractual lock-up tranche on Figma stock -- about 77.7 million shares, some 15% of the shares outstanding -- is released at the open on Friday 7 August 2026, two trading days after the 5 August second-quarter report; the overhang ends permanently, but at $24.32 (31 July close), after a 46% rally off the $16.60 record low, the upside to the $29 target is smaller than the drop back to that low.
dated_milestone: Friday 7 August 2026 -- the final extended lock-up tranche of approximately 77.7 million Class A shares (35% of the extended block, which covers about 54.1% of Class A stock) is released at the commencement of trading on the second trading day after the second-quarter 2026 earnings announcement, per the agreement of 30 August 2025 disclosed in the company's 8-K; the backstop date is 31 August 2026. The earnings announcement that sets the clock is Wednesday 5 August 2026, after the US close, confirmed by the company on 15 July 2026.
forcing_function:
The catalyst is a pair of dates in the same week, and they must be read together.

Wednesday 5 August 2026, after the close: the second-quarter report, against the company's own guide of $348.0-350.0 million (about 40% growth) and a raised full-year range of $1.422-1.428 billion with $125-135 million of adjusted operating income. This print settles the only question that matters for the terminal value: is net dollar retention still near the 139% posted in the March quarter, or has the generative-artificial-intelligence displacement fear started to appear in the customer numbers? Four public quarters, four met-or-beaten guides, with growth accelerating 38% to 40% to 46%, argue they hold the line -- but the market has repriced this stock 16.5% in a week on somebody else's product launch, so the print alone does not settle the price.

Friday 7 August 2026, at the open: the mechanical event. About 77.7 million shares become sellable and the extended lock-up terminates for good. This is the last of four tranches and the largest. After it, Figma has no contractual supply overhang for the first time in its public life.

What forces the re-rating is the combination -- a clean print followed by the market discovering that the release does not produce the flood it feared. That combination is genuinely powerful, and it is also genuinely unknowable four days ahead of it. The third, undated forcing function is the Findell Capital campaign: an independent board review of the competitor conflict, or an announced cut of the product line from eight to four with a stock-compensation reduction, would re-rate the stock on its own.
consensus_delta:
Where we disagree with the market runs in both directions, and that two-sidedness is itself the reason to wait rather than to buy.

The street is wrong on demand. The tape prices Figma as a business being deleted by generative artificial intelligence: down about 83% from the August 2025 peak of $142.92, and at the July low the operating business was valued at roughly 5 times this year's revenue. That is a terminal-decline price. The company's own numbers say the opposite. Revenue growth went 38% in the September 2025 quarter, 40% in December, then 46% in March 2026 -- it accelerated straight through the months the displacement narrative was being written. Net dollar retention reached 139%, the highest in over two years, meaning existing customers spent 39% more than a year earlier. If artificial intelligence were dissolving this business, retention is the first place it would appear, and it has gone the other way. Full-year guidance was raised, not trimmed.

The street is also wrong on the plumbing, and in the same direction. Much of the analyst commentary treats the January 2026 lock-up expiry as the end of the supply story. It was not. The 30 August 2025 agreement layered four further releases on top of it, and the largest -- about 77.7 million shares -- has not happened yet. Anyone modelling the float as settled is modelling the wrong float.

But here is where we disagree with the bulls, including our own board file. The consensus that has formed in the last four weeks -- double bottom, reinstated Buy, activist target of $40 -- has already moved the price 46% off the low. Our target is $29.00; the street mean is $30.40 and falling (it was about $40 in March), on a rating book of four Buys, one Outperform and eight Holds. We are no longer meaningfully more bullish than the street on the destination. We are only earlier on the mechanism, and the mechanism arrives on 7 August whether we own the stock or not. Buying an insight the market has already partly discounted, four days ahead of the largest supply event in the company's history, is not expectations arbitrage. It is paying for the privilege of being right early.
valley_of_death:
The risky window is unusually short, unusually specific and four days away. It is a supply-and-sentiment problem, not a solvency one, and that distinction should be held firmly.

There is no cash-burn hump, no maturity wall and no covenant. Figma held $1.638 billion of cash and short-term investments at 31 March 2026 against $56.2 million of debt, almost all of it lease obligations, and generated about $237 million of free cash flow over the last four reported quarters. Cash was essentially flat across the last two quarters. Nothing about the next nine months threatens the company's ability to fund itself.

What can go wrong is price, in three overlapping ways.

First, the 5 August print. The guide is $348.0-350.0 million, about 40% growth. A number in line is already expected; the bar that matters is retention and the full-year range. Any softening -- retention slipping from 139%, or the $1.422-1.428 billion range merely reaffirmed rather than raised -- lands on a stock that has just risen 46% in four weeks and would hand the displacement narrative its first hard evidence.

Second, the 7 August release. About 77.7 million shares, roughly 15% of shares outstanding and a much larger fraction of the real float, become sellable at the open. The holders are venture funds that distribute in kind to limited partners who then sell without price sensitivity. The three earlier tranches each produced weeks of drift, not a one-day flush. Expect the pressure to run into late August at least.

Third, the sector. In the week to 24 July 2026 the shares fell about 16.5% on generative-artificial-intelligence displacement worry with no company-specific news whatsoever. That risk is exogenous, unhedgeable and can recur at any moment on a competitor's announcement.

And one slower drain that outlives all three: stock-based compensation ran $169.0 million in the March 2026 quarter, about half of revenue, and the share count rose about 10% over the year to 523.5 million. Even a perfect outcome on 5 and 7 August leaves roughly a tenth of the company being issued to employees annually. The lock-up ends; the dilution does not.
positioning_washout:
Forced selling is the entire thesis on this name, and for the first time it has a termination date rather than an open end. Understanding exactly who is selling is what separates the good version of this trade from the bad one.

The sellers are not disappointed fundamental holders and not a yield-focused base being forced out by a dividend cut. They are pre-listing venture funds and early employees. Venture funds rarely sell in the ordinary sense: they distribute shares in kind to their limited partners -- pension plans, endowments, funds of funds -- who then liquidate on their own timetable, often through a broker with instructions to complete rather than to achieve a price. That flow is genuinely price-insensitive, which is why it can push a stock far below any reasonable value and why it takes weeks to clear rather than days.

The sequence so far: the original 180-day lock-up expired 27 January 2026, freeing roughly two-thirds of the share count. On top of it, four staged tranches of the 54.1% extended block released about 38.9 million shares in November 2025, 44.4 million in February 2026 and 61.1 million in May 2026. Each was followed by drift. The stock made its record low of $16.60 in early July, about six weeks after the May tranche -- which is roughly how long that supply took to work through.

The employee side is a distinct and colder story. Staff watched roughly 80% of the paper value of their holdings evaporate between the August 2025 peak and the January 2026 unlock, when the stock was near $22.51. That cohort is not selling to take profits; it is selling to salvage. That behaviour is insensitive to the fundamental case and to good news.

What happens after 7 August is the honest open question. The optimistic reading is that the last identified seller is released, the register turns over to fundamental holders, and the drift ends. The realistic reading is that release is not exhaustion -- the shares merely become sellable, and the distribution-to-limited-partner chain then runs for weeks. The washout that would make this a buy is the tape from roughly 7 to 21 August: heavy volume, a decisive break of the $16.60-18.00 shelf, and then a failure to make a new low. That is a specific, observable event, and it has not happened.
moderator_conclusion:
This is a genuine, dated, binding event on a better business than the tape says -- and it is still not a buy today, for reasons of price and sequence rather than doubt.

Start with what is verified. The extended lock-up agreement of 30 August 2025 covers about 54.1% of Figma's Class A shares and releases in four tranches tied to earnings dates. Three have gone. The fourth and largest, about 77.7 million shares or roughly 15% of the shares outstanding, is released at the open on the second trading day after the June-quarter report, or 31 August 2026 if that comes first. The company confirmed on 15 July 2026 that it reports after the close on Wednesday 5 August. The release date is therefore Friday 7 August 2026. That is a hard, dated, contractual catalyst, and it is four days from now.

Now the two problems.

The first is direction. The board file describes this as forced-seller supply clearing. On 3 August the supply has not cleared; it has not even arrived. What 7 August delivers is permission to sell, and the sellers are venture funds that distribute stock in kind to limited partners who then liquidate without regard to price. Every prior tranche produced weeks of drift rather than a clean flush. The clearing this thesis needs is an empirical event that follows the contractual one by some unknown number of weeks -- and buying today means owning the position through it rather than after it.

The second is price, and it is the one that settles this. The board file's target of $29.00, floor of $17.50 and reward-to-risk of 2.85 are only mutually consistent at a share price near $20.49. Since that file was struck the stock has rallied about 46% off its $16.60 record low to close at $24.32 on 31 July. Against the verified $16.60 low, the same $29.00 target now offers about 19% up against about 32% down: roughly 0.6 to 1, pointing the wrong way. Reconciling the two cases gives a probability-weighted value of about $23 -- slightly below where the stock already trades. There is no margin of safety left at this entry, which is why the value score here is a 2 despite a business I like: the downside is demonstrated rather than defined, net cash is only about $3.00 a share against a $24.32 price, and nothing contractual defends the level.

What I do like, and it is not nothing. Revenue growth accelerated from 38% to 40% to 46% across the last three reported quarters, precisely while the market priced obsolescence. Net dollar retention hit 139%, the best in over two years. Full-year guidance was raised to $1.422-1.428 billion with $125-135 million of adjusted operating income. Free cash flow ran about $237 million over four quarters against $1.638 billion of cash and effectively no debt. An engaged activist is pushing for the product line to be cut from eight to four and for a board investigation into a competitor conflict, and the market applauded the letter. If the 5 August print holds the line on retention, the case for $29-30 is sound.

So: wait for the wash-out, and here is the specific wash-out rather than a vague one. Two conditions, both observable. First, the 5 August report must show revenue at or above the guided $348-350 million with retention holding near 139%. Second, the tape from 7 August through roughly the third week of the month must absorb the release -- heavy volume, and either a hold above $20 or a break toward the $16.60-18.00 shelf that then fails to make a new low. Re-underwrite below about $20.10, where the reward-to-risk against the $29 target restores to roughly 2.5 to 1 and this becomes the position the board file thought it was buying. Above $24 it is not.

The operating moat is narrow but holding -- shared multiplayer design files are where whole product teams live, and 139% retention is the direct evidence. The threat from generative artificial intelligence collapsing the cost of good-enough design output is material to the multiple and is not yet visible in the customer numbers. Gross margin falling from about 92% to 79.4%, stock compensation near half of revenue, and a share count up about 10% in a year are the real costs of defending that position, and they are why this is a trade around an event rather than a franchise to own through anything.
interrogator_dossier:
# FIG (Figma, Inc.) -- Forensic dossier: a forced-seller special situation

Event-driven review, verified live on 3 August 2026. The question in front of this committee is not whether Figma is a good business. It is whether the gap between Friday's close of $24.32 and a plausible event-resolved value is wide enough, and whether the event that is supposed to close that gap is real, dated and pointed in the right direction.

The short answer, established below and then tested in every section: the event is real, it is contractually dated to Friday 7 August 2026, and it is the largest single release of stock in the company's short public life. But it is a supply event arriving into a price that has already risen about 46% off its record low in four weeks. The asymmetry the board file was underwriting has been spent by the rally, and the supply has not yet landed.

## 1. Narrative arc -- how the setup got here

Figma listed on the New York Stock Exchange on 31 July 2025 at $33 a share and traded to an intraday $142.92 in its first weeks. It closed Friday 31 July 2026 at $24.32. That is roughly 83% below the peak and about 26% below the offering price, on a business whose revenue has grown every single quarter since.

That divergence is the whole reason this name is in front of us, and it has two causes that must be kept separate because they call for opposite conclusions.

The first cause is plumbing. Figma came public with a very small tradable float and a lock-up (the window during which insiders and pre-listing investors are barred from selling) that was unusually elaborate. The original 180-day lock-up ran out on 27 January 2026, releasing roughly two-thirds of the share count. Layered on top of that, an agreement signed on 30 August 2025 with holders of about 54.1% of the Class A shares set up a second, staggered release running through 2026. Each tranche is tied to an earnings announcement: about 38.9 million shares (17.5% of the block) after the third-quarter 2025 report, released November 2025; about 44.4 million (20%) after the full-year 2025 report, released February 2026; about 61.1 million (27.5%) after the first-quarter 2026 report, released May 2026; and about 77.7 million (35%) at the open on the second trading day after the second-quarter 2026 report, or 31 August 2026 if that comes first -- pending, and dated 7 August 2026.

Figma confirmed on 15 July 2026 that it will report the June quarter after the close on Wednesday 5 August 2026. Two trading days later is Friday 7 August 2026. That is the date. It is not an estimate, a guidance range or a management aspiration; it is a contractual trigger disclosed in a filed 8-K, and the only way it moves is if the earnings date moves, in which case the backstop of 31 August 2026 applies.

The second cause is a genuine argument about the future. Since roughly April 2026 the market has been pricing design software as a category that generative artificial intelligence may make cheap or unnecessary. A competitor's launch of a rival design tool in April 2026 is the specific event that crystallised that fear for this stock. In the week to 24 July 2026 the shares fell about 16.5% on nothing company-specific -- an industry-wide de-rating of software on artificial-intelligence displacement worry. The record low of $16.60 was printed in early July.

The rally back to $24.32 came from three things: a double bottom in the chart around $16.60-18.00, a reinstated Buy from Bank of America, and an activist campaign that put a $40 target on the tape. None of those is the lock-up.

The arc, stated plainly: a healthy business was repriced by a combination of mechanical supply and a legitimate secular fear, and it has already bounced hard into the last, largest tranche of that supply.

## 2. Is the catalyst real, dated and binding?

Yes on all three counts, with one important qualification.

Real and dated. The release is documented in the 8-K covering the 30 August 2025 extended lock-up agreement. The trigger is mechanical. The date, 7 August 2026, is four days from now.

Binding. The holders are released; nothing compels them to sell. That is the qualification, and it cuts in a specific direction that the bull case usually gets backwards. The event that is contractually certain is the arrival of permission to sell. What the thesis actually needs is the exhaustion of the sellers, and that is not contractual at all. It is an empirical question about how quickly roughly 77.7 million shares -- about 15% of the ~528 million shares outstanding, and a far larger fraction of the shares that actually trade -- are absorbed.

Who the sellers are. These are pre-listing venture funds. They generally do not sell in the ordinary sense; they distribute shares in kind to their limited partners, who then liquidate on their own schedule with no reference to price. That is why this pressure has historically taken weeks rather than a day to clear, and why the three earlier tranches each produced a drift lower rather than a single clean flush.

What this means for direction. A forced-seller trade pays when the seller is exhausted, not when the seller is released. Buying on 3 August is buying four days ahead of the supply, not after it. The board file's own framing -- forced-seller supply clearing -- describes a state this name has not yet reached.

## 3. Sponsor and management credibility on hitting the date

There is no sponsor to handicap here, and that is a point in the setup's favour: no acquirer can walk, no regulator can issue a second request, no trial can miss its endpoint. The date arrives on its own.

Management credibility matters for the other event in the same week -- the 5 August earnings report -- and the record there is good but short. The December 2025 quarter delivered $303.8 million with growth reaccelerating to 40% from 38%. The March 2026 quarter delivered $333.4 million, up 46%, with adjusted earnings of $0.10 a share against $0.06 expected. Full-year 2026 guidance was raised to $1.422-1.428 billion, about 35% growth, and adjusted operating income guidance lifted to $125-135 million. The June quarter, reported 5 August, is guided to $348.0-350.0 million, about 40% growth.

Four quarters of public guidance, four met or beaten, with the growth rate going 38% to 40% to 46% rather than the other way. Net dollar retention -- how much existing customers spend this year versus last -- reached 139% in the first quarter of 2026, the highest in over two years. On the narrow question of whether they hit their own number on 5 August, the honest answer is that they probably will. Reliability: high, on a short record.

## 4. The verified downside floor -- what actually backstops the price

This is where the setup is weakest, and the committee should not be talked out of it.

There is no hard floor. This is not a merger with a signed agreement, not a company trading below net cash, not a liquidation. The balance sheet at 31 March 2026 held $1.638 billion of cash and short-term investments against $56.2 million of debt (almost all lease obligations), which is net cash of about $1.58 billion, or roughly $3.00 a share. At $24.32, cash accounts for 12% of the price. It backstops nothing.

What actually sits underneath the price is a valuation floor and a chart floor. The printed low is $16.60, struck in early July 2026 and re-tested to form the double bottom -- three weeks old and therefore a live, verified level rather than a historical curiosity. At that price the market capitalisation is about $8.8 billion and, net of cash, the operating business is valued at roughly $7.2 billion -- about 5.0 times this year's guided revenue and about 4.1 times the roughly $1.76 billion the street models for 2027. For a business compounding revenue in the high-30s with 139% net dollar retention, that is a price that requires the terminal-value argument to be true.

So the floor is real in the sense that the market recently paid it, and soft in the sense that nothing contractual stops the price going through it. Under the house rule that a special situation needs a defined downside, this one does not fully qualify: it has a demonstrated downside, which is a weaker thing. The board file carries the floor at $17.50; the verified level is $16.60, and I use that -- the more conservative and the more recently printed of the two.

## 5. Red flags

The spread has already closed. This is the single most important finding. The board file underwrites a target of $29.00, a floor of $17.50 and a reward-to-risk multiple of 2.85. Those three numbers are only mutually consistent at a share price of about $20.49, which is roughly where the stock traded when the file was struck. At Friday's $24.32 the same target and the verified $16.60 floor give about 19% of upside against about 32% of downside -- a ratio of roughly 0.6 to 1, against us. The rally did not confirm the thesis; it consumed it.

The supply is ahead of us, not behind us. The largest of the four tranches lands on 7 August, into a stock that has just risen 46% in four weeks. Every prior tranche produced weeks of drift.

Permanent dilution continues after the lock-up ends. The share count rose from 474.8 million in the first quarter of 2025 to 523.5 million in the first quarter of 2026, about 10% in a year. Stock-based compensation was $169.0 million in the first quarter of 2026 alone, roughly 51% of that quarter's revenue; the activist's own estimate for the full year is 27% of revenue against 8% at Adobe. So the bull sentence that the overhang clears for good on 7 August is wrong in an important way: the contractual overhang clears; the structural issuance of roughly a tenth of the company a year does not.

Gross margin has compressed materially. Reported gross margin has fallen from about 92% in late 2024 to 79.4% in the first quarter of 2026. Part of that is post-listing stock compensation landing in cost of revenue, but part is the cost of serving artificial-intelligence features, and that part does not reverse. A design-software business that used to convert 92 cents of every revenue dollar into gross profit and now converts about 80 is a structurally different business.

The accounting loss is large. The trailing twelve months show a net loss of about $1.40 billion on $1.16 billion of revenue. Most of that is the one-time listing-related stock charge of $1.14 billion booked in the September 2025 quarter, so it overstates the ongoing problem -- but even excluding it, the company loses money on a reported basis while guiding to $125-135 million of adjusted operating income. The entire gap is stock compensation.

The secular fear is not imaginary. The stock fell 16.5% in a single week in late July on artificial-intelligence displacement worry with no company news. That is a market that will re-price this name on a headline about somebody else's product, regardless of what Figma reports.

## 6. Green flags

The demand evidence contradicts the displacement narrative -- so far. Growth reaccelerated from 38% to 40% to 46% across the last three reported quarters, precisely while the market was pricing obsolescence. Net dollar retention hit a two-year high of 139%. If artificial intelligence were eating this business, it would show up here first, and it has not.

Cash generation is real, not a projection. Free cash flow over the last four reported quarters totals about $237 million ($60.6m, $49.0m, $39.2m, $88.6m). Cash and short-term investments were essentially flat at $1.64-1.66 billion across the last two quarters. There is no burn hump, no maturity wall and no covenant. Whatever goes wrong here in the next nine months, it will not be solvency.

An engaged, credible activist with a specific programme. Findell Capital's June 2026 letter asks for the product line to go from eight offerings to four, for costs and stock compensation to be cut, and for an independent board investigation into whether a partner improperly used Figma's confidential information before launching a competing tool. Findell carries a $40 twelve-month target. The stock rose more than 6% on the letter -- the market wants the discipline. This is a second, undated catalyst that could still fire.

The private-market anchor. Adobe agreed in 2022 to pay $20 billion for Figma, and paid a $1 billion fee when regulators killed the deal. Figma's enterprise value today is about $11.3 billion on roughly three times the revenue it had then. That does not make $20 billion the right number, but it does establish that a strategic buyer once valued this asset far above the current tape.

## 7. Hidden signals

The analyst target has been walking down, not up: the mean price target fell from about $40 in March 2026 to roughly $30.40 in late July, and the rating book is now four Buys, one Outperform and eight Holds. The sell side is not the source of the bounce.

The 200-day average sits at $28.86 against a 50-day at $21.53. The rally has taken the price back into the gap between them, which is exactly the zone where a bounce most often stalls.

The activist's product complaint and the company's growth reacceleration point in opposite directions. Findell wants eight products cut to four; management's own explanation for the 46% growth quarter is international expansion and adoption of the new artificial-intelligence products. One of them is misreading the business, and the 5 August call is where that gets tested.

## 8. Capital-allocation verdict for the director

Trajectory: turning. The top line is strengthening -- accelerating growth, record retention, raised guidance. The economic model is not: gross margin down about 13 points, stock compensation around half of revenue, a share count growing 10% a year, and a product portfolio the largest outside shareholder wants cut in half. Figma is mid-transformation from a single-product design tool into a multi-product artificial-intelligence suite, and the market is refusing to pay for the attempt.

Moat: narrow, and holding. The lock-in is genuine -- shared multiplayer design files are where whole product teams live, and 139% net dollar retention is the direct evidence that customers are deepening rather than leaving. But this is workflow habit rather than hard contractual lock-in, the kind of moat the current wave of generative tools is best at attacking, and the margin compression shows the moat is not free to defend. It is not wide, and on the evidence in hand it is not yet eroding either.

Secular threat: material, not terminal. Generative artificial intelligence collapsing the cost of good-enough design output is a live threat to pricing power, and the market has already voted. But the company's own retention and growth numbers currently point the other way, so this is a risk to the multiple more than to the existence of the business.

The single thing the director must weigh before sizing: the reward-to-risk that justified this name has already been paid out by the rally. At $24.32 you are risking about 32% to the verified $16.60 low to make about 19% to the $29.00 target, four days ahead of the largest release of stock in the company's public life. The event is genuine and its date is certain; the entry price is not the one the board file underwrote. Wait for the supply, then decide.
